title: How do we know? Finding out by noticing and testing
source: DeepKids Combined, The Deep End: a DeepKids topic from the DeepKids Grade 1 concept grid (Fringe Science: wild ideas must be tested, not just imagined). No board teaches it at this class, so there are no board subtopics to cover. No textbook needed.
summary: How do you know the Moon is not following you, or that blowing on a die does not bring a six? You test it. Your child learns what scientists do: notice, ask a question, make a guess they can test, test it fairly, repeat it, and tell others. They drop a full and a nearly empty bottle together, test the 'lucky blow' on a die, and watch mould grow in sealed bags. They hear true stories: Alexander Fleming's mouldy dish that led to penicillin, Mary Anning, a poor girl whose fossils changed science while others took the credit, Alfred Wegener, who was laughed at for saying the continents move and turned out right, and C.V. Raman, who tested a famous scientist's idea about why the sea is blue. They learn three questions to ask about any claim, including ours: Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?
builds_on: This is the first rung. It needs only a child who asks 'why?'. Class 3 adds fair tests with a control, claims that can never be tested, and the people left out of discovery stories. Class 5 adds blind tests, repeating other people's experiments, and how science checks itself.
subconcepts: science is a way of finding out, not a list of answers
observation: noticing carefully with all the senses
a question and a guess you can test (hypothesis)
a fair test: change only one thing
evidence: what we can see, count or measure
repeat it: one try is not enough
changing your mind when the evidence changes
Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?
wild ideas must be tested: some win, most don't
mistakes and accidents that led to discoveries
who found it, and who got the credit
goals: By the end your child can say what scientists do: notice, wonder, guess, test, repeat and share.
By the end your child can turn a 'why?' into a guess they can test, and test it fairly by changing only one thing.
By the end your child can explain why one try is not enough, using their own dice results.
By the end your child can ask 'Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?' about a claim.
By the end your child can tell the story of Mary Anning or Alfred Wegener and say why people did not believe them at first.
By the end your child can sort statements into true, false and 'scientists disagree or don't know yet'.
words: a way of finding out how the world works by looking, testing and checking
to notice carefully, with eyes, ears, nose, hands and tongue
something you want to find out
something you do to see if your guess is right
a test where you change only one thing
what you see, count or measure that tells you if something is true
the bones, shell or print of a living being from long ago, kept in rock
finding out something nobody knew before
a fuzzy fungus that grows on old food
when every one of a kind of animal or plant has died, so none are left
being thanked and named for something you did

days.title: Does the Moon follow you?
days.goal: Find out that we can check what we believe, starting with the Moon.

steps.title: How do you know?
steps.do: Ask three questions. After each answer, ask 'How do you know?' 'Is it day or night now?' (I can see the sky is light.) 'Is the milk hot?' (I touched the glass. I saw steam.) 'Is the Moon in the sky right now?' (I don't know. I would have to look.) Say: 'Each time you said I saw, I touched or I heard, you were using evidence. Evidence is what we can see, hear, count or measure. Some things we know, some we guess, and some we don't know yet.' Write three words on a big sheet: KNOW, GUESS, DON'T KNOW YET.

steps.title: Story: The Moon That Came Along
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). Don't explain yet why the Moon seems to follow. Ask: 'Arun thought the Moon was following only him. How did they find out it wasn't?' (They phoned Paati far away, and she saw it too.) 'The trees rushed past, but the far hill moved slowly. Why do you think that was?'

steps.title: Know, guess, don't know yet
steps.do: Say each sentence. Your child points to KNOW, GUESS or DON'T KNOW YET on the sheet. 'The Sun will rise tomorrow.' (Know: it has risen every day, because the Earth keeps spinning.) 'It will rain tomorrow.' (Guess.) 'There are animals on other planets.' (Don't know yet: nobody knows.) 'Our cat loves us.' (Guess: how could we test it?) 'Ice melts in the sun.' (Know: we have seen it many times.) Say: 'Scientists move things from GUESS to KNOW by testing. They are also honest about DON'T KNOW YET.' Then start the Wonder Wall project: your child says three things they wonder about. Write each on a slip and stick it on a wall or door.

need: sticky notes or paper slips and tape

days.title: Noticing, and a guess you can test
days.goal: Practise careful observation and turn a 'why' into a test.

steps.title: The ten-things walk
steps.do: Walk round your home, balcony or building for 10 minutes. Your child notices ten things, using at least four senses: the smell of the kitchen, a crow calling, a rough wall, a line of ants. For each one, ask: 'What do you wonder about it?' Write down one 'why' question for each. Say: 'To observe is to notice carefully. This is what scientists do first. Most people walk past a line of ants. A scientist stops and looks.'

steps.title: Heavy and light: which lands first?
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. First ask: 'If I drop a full bottle of water and a nearly empty one at the same time, which will land first? Why do you think so?' Write down your child's guess. A guess you can test is called a hypothesis. Drop the bottles together from shoulder height, five times. Your child listens: one thud or two? Then drop a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled one. Ask: 'Was your guess right? Why did the flat paper fall slowly?' (Air pushes up on it.)

steps.title: Start the mould garden
steps.do: Set up Experiment e3. Sprinkle a few drops of water on a slice of bread, a piece of idli and a piece of orange peel. Put each in its own zip bag, seal it and tape it shut. Ask: 'What do you think will happen in a week? Why?' Your child draws the three foods as they look today. Say: 'We will look again on Day 4 and Day 7, without opening the bags.'

need: two same-size plastic bottles with caps: one full of water, one with only a little water
a slice of bread, a piece of idli, orange peel

days.title: Does blowing on the die bring a six?
days.goal: Learn the fair test and why one try is never enough.

steps.title: Lucky things
steps.do: Ask: 'Do you have a lucky thing? A lucky pencil, a lucky shirt?' Many people believe that blowing on a die before throwing brings a six. Ask: 'How could we find out if that's true?' Listen to their idea. Good answers: throw it lots of times with blowing and lots without, and count.

steps.title: The dice test
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Throw the die 20 times without blowing and 20 times with blowing, the same way each time, onto the same tray. Your child makes a tally mark for every six. Ask before you start: 'What must stay the same so the test is fair?' (Same die, same tray, same way of throwing. The only change is the blowing.) After 5 throws each, stop and ask: 'Can we decide now?' After 20 each, compare. Usually each way gets about three or four sixes, and the numbers change from one try to the next.

steps.title: One try is not enough
steps.do: Ask: 'If your cousin blew on the die once and got a six, would that prove blowing works?' (No: you can get a six by chance. You need many throws.) 'If our test showed no difference, should we tell the cousin they're wrong?' (We can say what our evidence shows, and invite them to test it too.) Write on the big sheet: FAIR TEST = change only one thing. REPEAT IT = one try is not enough. Add to the Wonder Wall any new questions.

days.title: Happy accidents
days.goal: See how mistakes and accidents, noticed carefully, became discoveries.

steps.title: Mould garden check
steps.do: Look at the three sealed bags from Experiment e3 without opening them. Your child draws what they see. Are there fuzzy patches? What colours? Which food has the most? If nothing has grown yet, look again tomorrow. Ask: 'Where did the mould come from? We didn't put any in.' (Tiny mould spores, too small to see, float in the air all the time. They landed on the food before we sealed it.)

steps.title: The mould that saved lives
steps.do: Tell this true story. 'In 1928 a scientist in London, Alexander Fleming, came back from a holiday to his untidy lab. He had left out small glass dishes with bacteria growing in them. Bacteria are living beings too small to see, and some of them make us ill. One dish had a blue-green mould on it by mistake. Most people would have thrown it away. But Fleming noticed something odd: around the mould, the bacteria had died. He asked why. The mould made a chemical that kills bacteria. Years later it became the medicine penicillin.' Ask: 'What was the mistake? What turned the mistake into a discovery?' (Fleming noticed, and asked why.) Then add: 'Fleming could not make enough penicillin to use as a medicine. About 12 years later, a team in Oxford did it. One of them, Norman Heatley, built the equipment out of milk churns and bedpans. Who should get the credit?'

steps.title: Oops paintings
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Each of you drops a blob of paint on paper, folds the paper, presses and opens it. Turn the accidental shape into something: a butterfly, a monster, a map. Your child says one thing they noticed that they did not plan. Say: 'An accident only becomes a discovery when someone notices it and asks a question.'

days.title: The girl who found dragons
days.goal: Hear how a poor girl's evidence changed science, and who got the credit.

steps.title: Mary Anning
steps.do: Talk about voice v1. Tell it as a story: 'Mary Anning was born in 1799 in a seaside town in England called Lyme Regis. Her family was poor. She and her brother Joseph searched the crumbling cliffs for stone shells and bones to sell to visitors. In 1811 Joseph found a huge skull. About a year later Mary, aged about 12, found the rest of the skeleton. It belonged to a giant sea animal with a long snout and huge eyes, an ichthyosaur (say ik-thee-oh-sor). People thought it was a crocodile. It was not. It was a kind of animal that no longer lives anywhere: it was extinct. Finds like hers showed that whole kinds of animals can die out for ever.' Ask the voice question. Then say: 'Rich men bought her fossils and wrote about them, often without her name. She could not join the Geological Society, the club of scientists in London, because women were not allowed.' Ask: 'When only their names are written down, who is missing from the story?'

steps.title: Make a fossil
steps.do: Press a shell, a leaf or a toy dinosaur's foot into a flat ball of atta dough or clay, lift it out, and leave the print to dry. Say: 'A fossil is often a print like this, or bones that slowly turned to stone. They stay for millions of years in mud that became rock. Mary Anning learned to read them.' Ask: 'If someone finds your fossil in a million years, what could they tell about the thing that made it? What couldn't they tell?' (They could tell its shape and size. They could not tell its colour or its sound.)

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws1 (core). Read each item aloud. For the 'why' items, they say the answer and you write it. For every answer ask: 'How do you know?'

need: a handful of atta dough or clay

days.title: Wild ideas and 'Says who?'
days.goal: Meet wild ideas that won, see that famous people can be wrong, and play True, False or Scientists Disagree.

steps.title: The map puzzle
steps.do: Do Activity a2: cut out South America and Africa from a printed world map and slide them together. Ask: 'What do you notice?' (They fit like jigsaw pieces.) 'If they fitted together long ago, what must have happened?' Let your child guess before you tell them anything.

steps.title: Alfred Wegener's wild idea
steps.do: Talk about voice v3, Alfred Wegener, and ask its question. Say: 'He had a wild idea. Wild ideas are welcome in science, but they must be tested. His idea was tested for about 50 years, and the evidence showed he was mostly right. Most wild ideas turn out wrong.' Ask: 'What else could explain why the coasts fit?' (It could be chance. That is why he also looked for the same fossils and rocks on both sides of the ocean.)

steps.title: Why is the sea blue? Says who?
steps.do: Talk about voice v2, C.V. Raman on the ship. Ask: 'A very famous scientist said the sea is blue because it reflects the sky. Raman didn't just believe it. What did he do?' (He tested it: he blocked the sky's reflection and the sea was still blue.) Teach the three questions with a hand sign for each: 'Says who?' (point outward), 'How do they know?' (tap your eyes), 'Who's missing?' (open your hands). Say: 'Ask them of everyone. Of teachers. Of books. Of me.'

steps.title: True, False or Scientists Disagree?
steps.do: Play the card game (g1). Each player takes a card, reads it (or you read it), and puts it under TRUE, FALSE or SCIENTISTS DISAGREE OR DON'T KNOW. Before turning it over, they say how they know, or how someone could find out. Turn it over. Talk about the surprises: some dinosaurs are still alive, because birds are dinosaurs, and scientists still argue about whether trees talk.

prep.task: Print a world map and the game cards, and cut the cards out

days.title: I can find out
days.goal: Review, finish the Wonder Wall project and teach it back.

steps.title: Mould garden: last look
steps.do: Look at the sealed bags one last time (Experiment e3). Ask: 'Which food grew the most mould? Was your guess from Day 2 right? What would you change to make it a fair test?' (Same size pieces, all equally wet, same place.) Then throw the bags away still sealed.

steps.title: Stretch and challenge
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws2 (stretch), and, if they are keen, two or three items from Worksheet ws3 (challenge), with you reading aloud. On the challenge 'what if' items, take any well-reasoned answer.

steps.title: Test one wonder
steps.do: Do the last part of the project: your child picks one question from the Wonder Wall that you can test at home (for example 'Do ants like sugar more than salt?' or 'Which paper boat floats longest?'). Together, write: My question, My guess, How I'll test it fairly, What happened. Do the test now if it is quick. Look at Worksheet ws3 together for one of its puzzles if there's time.

steps.title: Check and teach it back
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud. Then your child teaches it back: they explain to another family member what scientists do (notice, wonder, guess, test, repeat, share), using the dice test as an example, and ask them the three questions: 'Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?'

sections.p: Science is mostly…

a way of finding out by looking, testing and checking

To find out if something is true, we look for ____: things we can see, count or measure.
Match the step to what it means.

tell others so they can check

sections.p: We want to know if blowing on a die brings more sixes. What is fair?
opts: throw many times with blowing and many times without, the same way
use a different die each time

sections.p: Your friend got a six once after blowing on the die. This proves…

the Moon will be in the sky tonight

Mary Anning found the fossils, but rich men wrote about them, often without her name. Was that fair? Why or why not?
Meenakshi, a girl in Class 1, says, 'My tulsi plants grow better when I sing to them.' Which test is fairest?

sing to a big plant and look at a small one

To be sure, scientists do a test again and again. This is called ____ the test.
A full bottle of water and a nearly empty bottle of the same size are dropped together. They…
opts: the full one lands much sooner
the nearly empty one floats down slowly

sections.p: Is it something you could test at home?
items: Do ants like sugar more than salt?
Does ice melt faster in the sun or shade?

sections.p: Raman tested a famous scientist's idea about the blue sea and found it was not the whole story. This shows…

sections.p: Wegener's idea that continents move was laughed at, but it was right. Should we believe every wild idea? What should we do with it instead?
Write one question from your Wonder Wall and how you could test it fairly.
A feather and a hammer were dropped together on the Moon, where there is no air. What happened?

the Moon makes its own light

Who gets their name written down in the story of a discovery?
opts: always the person who did the most work
often the person with more power, money or fame

sections.p: What if nobody was ever allowed to say 'I was wrong'? What would happen to science?
Your Paati (grandmother) says that when a crow caws at the door, guests are coming. How could you test it? What would you count?
Ask 'Who's missing?' about the penicillin story. Who helped that we usually forget?

experiments.title: Heavy and light: which lands first?
experiments.question: Do heavy things fall faster than light things?
need: two same-size plastic bottles with caps: one full of water, one with only a little water
steps: Your child says their guess and why. Write it down.
Stand on the floor, not a chair. Hold one bottle in each hand over the cushion, both at the same height, about as high as your shoulders.
Let go at exactly the same moment over the cushion. Listen: one thud or two?
Do it five times, taking turns to drop and to watch, because one try can be a fluke.
Now drop a flat sheet of paper and a crumpled sheet of paper together.
Last, put the flat sheet on top of a book and drop the book. Watch the sheet.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will land first, the full bottle or the nearly empty one? Why do you think so?'
experiments.observe: The two bottles land at the same moment, with one thud. The crumpled paper falls much faster than the flat sheet. The sheet on top of the book falls with the book.
experiments.why: Gravity is the force that pulls things down towards the Earth. It pulls harder on the full bottle. But the full bottle is also harder to get moving. The two cancel out, so both bottles fall at the same speed. Air pushes up on falling things. This is called air resistance. It hardly slows a bottle, but a flat sheet catches a lot of air and floats down. On top of the book, the book pushes the air out of the way. In 1971 the astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together on the Moon, where there is no air. They landed at the same time.
experiments.safety: Drop from standing height onto a cushion, away from toes and glass. Keep the caps tight. Don't climb on furniture.

experiments.title: The lucky-blow dice test
experiments.question: Does blowing on a die make a six more likely?
steps: Agree the rules: same die, same tray, shake in cupped hands and throw the same way every time.
Throw 20 times without blowing. Make a tally mark every time a six comes up.
Throw 20 times, blowing on the die in your hands before each throw. Tally the sixes.
After the first 5 throws of each, stop and compare. Then carry on to 20.
Compare the totals. If you have time, do 20 more of each and add them up.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will blowing give us more sixes? How many sixes do you expect out of 20 throws?'
experiments.observe: Both ways usually give about three or four sixes in 20 throws, but it changes: sometimes one, sometimes six. After only 5 throws the results can look very different. After 40 they get closer.
experiments.why: A fair die has six faces, so each face comes up about one time in every six throws, whatever you do before throwing. Small numbers of throws can look 'lucky' just by chance, which is why scientists repeat tests many times before deciding. Testing a belief fairly, instead of arguing about it, is the heart of science.

experiments.title: The sealed mould garden
experiments.question: Where does mould grow, and where does it come from?
need: a slice of bread, a piece of idli, a piece of orange peel
steps: Sprinkle a few drops of water on each food.
Put each in its own zip bag, seal it, and tape the seal shut.
Label the bags and leave them in a warm, dark cupboard.
Draw the food on Day 2, Day 4 and Day 7. Never open the bags. In cool weather the mould may take a few more days.
On Day 7, throw the bags in the bin still sealed.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will anything grow? Which food will grow the most?'
experiments.observe: In a few days, fuzzy patches of white, green, blue-green or black mould appear. They spread and change colour.
experiments.why: Moulds are fungi. Their spores, far too small to see, float in the air everywhere and land on food. With water, warmth and food, they grow into the fuzzy threads you see. One blue-green mould, Penicillium, makes a chemical that kills some bacteria: Alexander Fleming noticed this in 1928, and it became the medicine penicillin.
experiments.safety: Never open the bags or sniff the mould: the spores can make people ill, especially anyone with asthma or allergies. Throw them away sealed. Wash hands after handling.
experiments.time: 8 min, then 3 short checks over 5 days

activities.title: Oops paintings
steps: Drop a blob or two of paint in the middle of a sheet.
Fold the paper in half, press, and open it.
Look at the accidental shape. What does it remind you of?
Add eyes, legs, words or colour to turn it into something.
Give it a name and say one thing you noticed that you didn't plan.
activities.outcome: A painting made from an accident, and the idea that noticing turns an accident into a discovery.

activities.title: The continent jigsaw
steps: Find South America and Africa on the map.
Cut them out along the coast.
Slide them across the paper towards each other. Do they fit?
Look for other pieces that might fit.
Ask: 'If they fitted together long ago, what must have happened?'
activities.outcome: A map puzzle showing the clue that made Alfred Wegener think the continents had moved.

voices.idea: A poor fossil hunter from Lyme Regis who taught herself. With her brother Joseph she found the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be correctly identified (about 1811 to 1812), and later the first nearly complete plesiosaur (1823). Her finds were key evidence that some kinds of animals had gone extinct, and that the Earth's past was very long.
voices.then: Rich collectors and scientists bought her fossils and wrote about them, often without naming her. As a woman she could not join the Geological Society of London. When she found the plesiosaur, the famous French scientist Georges Cuvier at first thought it might be a fake, because its neck was so long. When he looked closely, he agreed it was real.
voices.now: She is now remembered as one of the great fossil hunters. In 2010 the Royal Society named her among the most influential British women in science, and in 2022 a statue of her was put up in Lyme Regis after a campaign started by a schoolgirl.
voices.ask: Cuvier thought the plesiosaur might be fake. What should he do before deciding: trust his feeling, trust Mary, or look at the bones?

voices.idea: In 1921, on a ship to England, Raman looked at the deep blue Mediterranean Sea. The famous scientist Lord Rayleigh had said the sea is blue mainly because it reflects the blue sky. Raman used a small prism that blocks reflected light, looked at the water, and it was still blue. He decided that water itself scatters light and makes the blue.
voices.then: He published his idea in 1921. It led him and his student K.S. Krishnan to a new discovery about how light scatters, the Raman effect, in 1928.
voices.now: Scientists agree that the sea's blue comes mostly from the water itself, which soaks up red light, and partly from scattering and the sky's reflection. Raman won the Nobel Prize in 1930. Krishnan, who worked with him on the discovery, was not included.
voices.ask: Raman checked an idea from a very famous scientist. Is it rude to test what a famous person says? Why or why not?

voices.idea: In 1912 Wegener said the continents were once joined in one giant land and have slowly drifted apart. His evidence: the coasts of Africa and South America fit, the same fossils and rocks are found on both sides of the ocean, and coal is found in icy Antarctica.
voices.then: Most geologists laughed. He could not explain what force could push whole continents, and he was a weather scientist, not a geologist.
voices.now: In the 1950s and 1960s, maps of the ocean floor (made with the help of Marie Tharp) and other evidence showed that the Earth's crust is made of plates that move a few centimetres a year. Wegener was mostly right. He died on an expedition in Greenland in 1930, before he was believed.
voices.ask: Wegener had good clues but no explanation of how. Were the other scientists wrong to doubt him? What would have convinced you?

check.q: What do scientists do to find out about the world?
check.a: They notice, wonder (ask a question), make a guess they can test, test it fairly, repeat it, and share it so others can check.
A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.

check.q: Why isn't one throw of a die enough to know if blowing on it works?
check.a: You can get a six by chance. You have to throw it many times each way and compare.

check.q: What are the three questions to ask about any claim?
check.a: Says who? How do they know? Who's missing?

check.q: How did a messy mistake help Alexander Fleming?
check.a: Mould grew on his dish by accident. He noticed that the bacteria around it had died, asked why, and found penicillin.

check.q: Who was Mary Anning and why do we tell her story?
check.a: A poor girl in England who found giant fossils. They showed that some kinds of animals had died out for ever. Others often took the credit, and she was not allowed to join the scientists' club.

check.q: Should we believe every wild idea? What should we do?
check.a: No: we should test it. Some wild ideas, like Wegener's moving continents, turn out right. Most turn out wrong.

project.title: The Wonder Wall
steps: On Day 1, start a Wonder Wall on a door or wall: every question your child wonders about goes on a slip.
Each day, add at least one new question from the walk, the tests or the stories.
Sort the slips into three groups: 'I can test it at home', 'I need to ask or read', and 'Nobody knows yet'.
On Day 7, pick one testable question. Write: My question, My guess, How I'll test it fairly, What happened.
Do the test and add the result to the wall, with a drawing.
Keep the wall going after this week: when a question is answered, ask 'How do we know?'
project.outcome: A wall of your child's own questions, sorted by how they could be answered, and one real fair test they designed and ran themselves.

game.title: True, False or Scientists Disagree?
rules: Put the three category cards face up in a row: TRUE, FALSE and SCIENTISTS DISAGREE OR DON'T KNOW. Shuffle the other cards face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it (a grown-up can read for younger players).
Put it under the category you think is right, and say how you know, or how someone could find out.
Turn it over. If you are right, keep it. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
If you gave a good 'how could we find out' even when wrong, you may keep it anyway, if the other players agree.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins. Then pick the most surprising card and talk about it.

cards.front: The Earth is shaped like a ball.
cards.back: TRUE (very slightly squashed at the top and bottom)

cards.front: The Sun goes round the Earth.
cards.back: FALSE: the Earth goes round the Sun

cards.front: The Earth spins round once in about a day.
cards.back: TRUE

cards.front: One trip of the Earth round the Sun takes one month.
cards.back: FALSE: it takes a year

cards.front: The Sun makes its own light.
cards.back: TRUE

cards.front: The Moon makes its own light.
cards.back: FALSE: it shines with reflected sunlight
TRUE: the closest star to us
TRUE: the land they sit on moves a few centimetres a year, and they rise and wear down
FALSE: air is matter and has weight

cards.front: The space around you is empty.
cards.back: FALSE: it is full of air
TRUE: tiny drops of water or bits of ice
TRUE: its tiny particles are always jiggling
TRUE: there is no biggest number

cards.front: Atoms are the smallest things and can never be split.
cards.back: FALSE: atoms are made of smaller parts and can be split
FALSE: birds are living dinosaurs
TRUE
TRUE: all mammals share ancestors, and all living things are related

cards.front: There are about as many bacteria living in and on you as there are cells in your body.
cards.back: TRUE: the best count says roughly equal
SCIENTISTS DISAGREE: plants sense touch and damage, and send warning signals through their bodies. Some scientists call this feeling. Others say pain needs a brain.

cards.front: Trees talk to each other through fungi in the soil.
cards.back: SCIENTISTS DISAGREE: fungi link the roots of trees and pass some food and signals between them. How much trees 'talk' is argued about.

cards.front: The universe has an edge you could reach.
cards.back: FALSE as far as we know: no edge has ever been found

cards.front: There is life on other planets.
cards.back: DON'T KNOW: nobody knows yet

cards.front: Space between faraway galaxies is stretching.
cards.back: TRUE: the universe is expanding
SCIENTISTS DISAGREE: in sleep, many animals' brains do what ours do when we dream. Many scientists think they dream. What they see, nobody knows.

big: How can you know something for sure? Is there anything you are completely sure of?
Is it brave or silly to believe a wild idea before anyone has tested it?
Your dog knows the world by smell, a bat by echoes. Are their kinds of knowing as good as ours?
If someone finds out something new but nobody writes their name down, did they still discover it?
Is it all right to say 'I don't know'? Who is braver: someone who says it, or someone who pretends?

challenge.q: Galileo is said to have dropped two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to show heavy and light things fall together. Did he?
challenge.hint: The story was told by his student Vincenzo Viviani many years later, and Galileo never described doing it, so many historians doubt it happened that way. A Dutch scientist, Simon Stevin, did report dropping two lead balls from a church tower in Delft in 1586, and they landed together. Galileo did real experiments with balls rolling down slopes. Ask: why might one famous name collect all the stories?

challenge.q: Many people say Columbus proved the Earth was round. Is that right?
challenge.hint: No. Educated people had known the Earth is round for about 2,000 years before Columbus. The Greek scholar Eratosthenes measured its size around 240 BCE using shadows, and in India Aryabhata wrote in 499 CE that the Earth spins. The argument with Columbus was about how big the Earth was, and he was wrong about that. Ask: how could you show a friend that the Earth is round, without a rocket?

challenge.q: Fleming discovered penicillin all by himself. True?
challenge.hint: Fleming noticed the mould in 1928, but he could not make enough of it to use as a medicine. In Oxford, Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and the lab helper Norman Heatley made it work about 12 years later. A lab worker in America, Mary Hunt, found a mouldy melon at a market, and its mould made much more penicillin. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize. Heatley and Hunt did not. Ask: who else should be in the story?

perspectives.who: A farmer in a Maharashtra village
perspectives.view: Many farmers say that when ants carry their eggs to higher ground, rain is coming. This is knowledge built from watching for years, though it is rarely written down. Ask: how could we test it? Who should get credit if it turns out true?

A dog finds out about the world mainly through their nose: who walked by, and what they ate. They know things we can't. Ask: is smelling a kind of evidence? What do we miss because we use mostly our eyes?

A detective doesn't just believe what people say. They look for clues, check stories against each other, and change their mind when a new clue turns up. Ask: how is a scientist like a detective? How is it different?
Babies drop spoons again and again and watch them fall. Some scientists say babies are little scientists, testing the world. Ask: what were you testing when you were a baby?

story.title: The Moon That Came Along
text: The night bus from Chennai to Madurai smelled of oranges, diesel and somebody's jasmine. Arun had the window seat because he was six and his sister Kavya was nine. Amma said that was the rule. Kavya said Amma had made the rule up on the spot.
The bus left the city, past the last petrol pump and the last tea stall, and the dark came up on both sides. Then Arun saw it. A huge, round, white Moon sat just above the hills.

He watched it for a long time. The bus went round a bend. The Moon came too. The bus climbed a slope. The Moon climbed with it. The bus stopped at a red light in a small town where one dog was asleep in the road, and the Moon stopped, and waited.
'Akka,' he whispered. 'The Moon is following me.'
Kavya did not look up from her book. 'It's following me,' she said. 'I'm older.'
'It's following me. It stopped when we stopped. I saw.'
'You can't both be right,' said Amma sleepily from the seat in front. 'Unless you are.'
This was the kind of thing Amma said, and it was very annoying.

Arun pressed his nose to the glass. The trees beside the road rushed past, whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, gone before he could count them. The electric poles flicked by like the ticks of a clock. But far away, a long dark hill with one light on top did not rush. It slid along slowly. And the Moon did not move at all. It just came along.
Kavya had put her book down. She was watching too.
'Here's a test,' she said, because she had just learned about tests at school. 'If the Moon is following you, then when you close your eyes it won't know where you are.'
Arun closed his eyes and counted to twenty. When he opened them, the Moon was right there, exactly where it had been.
'That proves it,' he said. 'It likes me.'
'That proves nothing,' said Kavya. 'Let's do another test.' She took Amma's phone, which she was not supposed to do, and called Paati.
Paati lived in Hyderabad, a whole night's train away in the other direction. She answered on the second ring, because she never slept before eleven.
'Paati,' said Kavya. 'Go outside and look at the sky. Is there a Moon?'
They heard the creak of Paati's terrace door, the slap of her chappals on the steps and somebody's television far off. Then Paati's voice came back, soft and surprised.
'Oh,' she said. 'Yes. It's big tonight. Round and white, just over the water tank. I'm sitting on my chair and it is sitting with me.'
Arun stared at the Moon outside the bus window. Then he stared at the phone.
'But it's here,' he said. 'It's with me.'
'It's with me too,' said Paati.
Nobody said anything for a while. The bus hummed. The trees went whoosh, whoosh. The far hill slid slowly. The Moon did not move at all.
Arun thought about the trees, which were close and rushed past. He thought about the hill, which was far and slid slowly. And he thought about the Moon, which did not move even a little.
'Akka,' he said slowly. 'What if close things seem to go fast, and far things seem to go slow, and the Moon is so far away that it doesn't seem to move at all?'
Kavya opened her mouth to say something clever, and closed it again.
'So far away,' said Arun, 'that it can be with me, and with Paati, and with that dog in the road, all at the same time.'
'That's a hypothesis,' said Kavya at last. 'A guess you can test.' But she said it in a quieter voice, not the voice for winning.
For a moment Arun felt a little sad. He had liked the Moon being his, like a secret friend. Then he looked out at the Moon again, and thought of Paati on her terrace, looking at the very same Moon.
'Paati,' he said. 'Can you see it now?'
'I can see it.'
'I'm looking at it too,' he said. 'So we're looking at the same thing.'
'We are,' said Paati.
They stayed on the phone a long time, not talking much: an old woman on a terrace in Hyderabad, and a small boy and his sister on a bus near Tiruchirappalli, all three of them looking up.
The Moon came along, all the way to Madurai.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the story turns twice. First, Arun's belief is tested with someone else's evidence: Paati, far away, sees the Moon 'following' her too, so it cannot be following only him. Then he notices that near things rush past and far things slide slowly, and guesses that the Moon is so far away that it hardly seems to move. That is a real explanation, called parallax, reached by noticing and guessing, and it is a hypothesis he could test. He also finds that the Moon is not his alone: everyone under the sky sees the same Moon.
ask: Arun thought the Moon was following only him. What evidence changed his mind?
Why did the trees rush past but the hill slide slowly?
Kavya said 'That's a hypothesis.' What was the guess, and how could you test it on your next car or bus ride?
How did Arun feel when he found out the Moon wasn't only his? Did the feeling change?
Who else in the whole world might have been looking at the same Moon that night?

ideas.idea: Science is a way of finding out, not a book of answers.
ideas.more: Anyone can do it: notice, wonder, guess, test, repeat and share. Show it with the dice test, where your child's own tally marks decide the answer, not a grown-up.

ideas.idea: Evidence beats 'because I said so', even from famous people.
ideas.more: Raman tested Lord Rayleigh's idea, and Mary Anning's bones beat the experts' doubts. Teach the three questions with hand signs: Says who? How do they know? Who's missing? And invite your child to ask them of you.

ideas.idea: Mistakes and wild ideas can be doors, if someone notices and tests them.
ideas.more: Fleming's messy dish became penicillin. Wegener's 'silly' idea became the science of moving plates. But most wild ideas turn out wrong, so they must be tested, not just believed.

ideas.idea: The story of a discovery is also a story of who was left out.
ideas.more: Mary Anning, Norman Heatley and K.S. Krishnan did real work and were often not named. Whenever you hear a discovery story, ask who else was there.

unknowns: How many kinds of living things share the Earth with us? Scientists have named about two million, but there may be many millions more that nobody has ever described.
Is there life anywhere else in the universe? Nobody knows yet, and scientists are looking.
Why do we dream, and do animals dream like us? Scientists have ideas but no one is sure.

books.title: Stone Girl, Bone Girl: The Story of Mary Anning
books.author: Laurence Anholt
books.why: A warm picture book of Mary Anning's life on the cliffs at Lyme Regis, to read after Day 5.

books.title: Ada Twist, Scientist
books.author: Andrea Beaty
books.why: A girl who never stops asking 'why?' and tests everything, which is exactly this week.

books.title: Rosie Revere, Engineer
books.author: Andrea Beaty
books.why: A girl whose flying machine crashes, and whose great-aunt cheers the failure. A good one for the day on mistakes.

books.author: Barney Saltzberg
